variants.name: async/await coroutine state
variants.idiom_name: async function + await (closure as the token)
variants.implementation_notes: JavaScript needs no explicit token: the closure passed to then(onFulfilled, onRejected) captures the per-operation state and settlement dispatches straight to it, and async/await is the same mechanism with the state held in the suspended coroutine - code after an await can be thought of as existing in a .then callback. Cancellation and correlation, which promises do not express, are separate carriers: AbortController/AbortSignal abandons an outstanding operation, Node's AsyncLocalStorage carries request-scoped state deeper in the call tree. A hand-written token map is only needed to bridge callback APIs into promises; use the ES2015 new Promise constructor, or Promise.withResolvers where an ES2024 runtime/lib is available.
pitfalls: Handlers are retained by a promise while it is pending and reachable: attaching handlers repeatedly to a promise that never settles, or forgetting to delete entries from a token map, is a memory leak.

An AbortController's AbortSignal becomes permanently aborted after abort(): reusing it makes later operations start already aborted, and listeners accumulate unless each request has its own controller or listeners use { once: true }.
An operation not yet awaited or .then-wired can reject unhandled even if a catch appears later in the same function - wire every concurrent operation (Promise.all/allSettled) before continuing.

AsyncLocalStorage loses its store across callback APIs and custom thenables (util.promisify/AsyncResource restore it), and enterWith() leaks the store for the rest of the synchronous execution - prefer run().

variants.name: then() continuation closure
variants.implementation_notes: Before async/await, the token was the continuation passed to then(), and it remains the right form where the completion must be handled without suspending a function: handlers registered on settlement are dispatched by the microtask queue, and chaining sequences steps without rewriting the caller as async. The costs are nesting and the wiring hazard - a promise whose rejection handler is attached only later can surface as an unhandled rejection first.
pitfalls: A rejection handler attached only after another await can arrive too late: the rejection is reported as unhandled first.
then() results must be returned or awaited; a discarded chain loses completion order, and the token's state is then unreachable from the caller.
